title: Knowledge-Building Isn’t Just for Students
author: Science of Reading Classroom
summary: A second-grade teacher argues that the science-of-reading movement has trained teachers in foundational skills through programs like LETRS but has not given them the content knowledge that knowledge-building curricula now require them to teach. She reads teacher complaints that such lessons are boring or too much as a symptom of the teachers own gaps in history, geography, and science, which their schooling and training also left unfilled. Her proposed fix is professional development in content areas, alongside a personal strategy of starting with a short overview book and deepening it each summer. She illustrates with her own work on the War of 1812, where her students loved a unit she had expected to bore them, and she then built real knowledge through reading, a teacher institute, and travel. The central move is to extend the knowledge-matters argument from students to the teaching profession.
points: Knowledge-building curricula put teachers in the position of teaching content they were never taught, and the frustration seen on teacher forums may reflect that gap rather than flawed lessons.
Teacher training addressed foundational reading skills but not the history, geography, and science content that now fills the literacy block, so PD in content knowledge is the next gap to close.
A practical self-education path is to begin with a short accessible overview and add deeper resources each summer, building knowledge year over year.
The teacher's own prejudice against a topic came from ignorance of it, and learning more transformed both her interest and her students engagement.
quotes: However, these programs did not get teachers up to speed on the knowledge-building content that they are being asked to teach. Many of us were denied a robust education in history, geography, science, and even literature in elementary and high school. We also did not receive this knowledge in teacher training.

Teaching content we barely know, with no schema for understanding its larger context, is both frustrating and uncomfortable. Teachers deserve instruction in these areas as well. I believe this is the next critical step in professional development and teacher training.

The speaker recommended starting with a short, accessible book that gave a broad overview of the topic. Then, each summer break, find more comprehensive, in-depth resources to build on that knowledge year after year.

I was shocked by their excitement about the content. But I realized my initial prejudice was based solely on my ignorance of the content, not the content itself. I had never learned about the War of 1812 in all my school career.

Teachers have access to countless resources for building their individual knowledge, but I believe that professional development in knowledge-building content areas is just as essential as training in foundational reading skills. Teachers are often expected to teach content they were never taught themselves, yet this knowledge is just as critical as understanding how to teach foundational reading skills.

Gilbert Highet, in The Art of Teaching, said it this way, “The first essential of good teaching, then, is that the teacher must know the subject. That really means that [she or] he must continue to learn it.
